design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (British Journal of Psychiatry 2009;194:355-359) at Hammersmith Hospital, London, comparing serotonin transporter binding with [11C]DASB and arterial input in three groups of men: 12 who had used MDMA on at least 25 occasions but not in the past year, 9 who used a range of other recreational drugs and had never used MDMA, and 19 who reported no illicit drug use. Binding potential was derived from the total distribution volume relative to cerebellum in 10 regions and compared by repeated-measures analysis of variance with age as covariate.
can_establish: That in these 40 men, transporter binding in the regions measured did not differ significantly between men who had stopped using MDMA at least a year earlier, men who used other drugs and men who used none, and that no variable of MDMA use correlated with binding.
cannot_establish: Whether binding had ever been lower in these men (no earlier scan and no group of people currently using MDMA); whether cortical binding is normal in regions other than frontal cortex (only frontal cortex was analysed, because of low signal); whether the groups are equivalent (a non-significant test in 12 against 19 people, with no regional values or intervals printed); or anything about women.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper or magazine advertisement and word of mouth; diagnostic assessment by psychiatrists using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (p. 355).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 25-60; no psychotropic medication; no major psychiatric or neurological problem; no history of drug dependence; no more than three units of alcohol in the 24 h before testing; no recreational drug use for at least 3 days before testing. MDMA group: at least 25 occasions of use, none for at least 1 year. Two people were excluded after hair analysis was positive for MDMA (p. 355).
sample.demographics: Men only. Mean age: no illicit drug use 30.5 (range 25-45), formerly used MDMA 28.2 (25-36), other drugs 35.6 (25-50); the groups differed (p=0.03), so age was a covariate. No group differences in depression, anxiety, neuroticism or premorbid IQ (p>0.2) (pp. 356-357).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one scan per person); 2 people excluded before analysis for MDMA-positive hair.
sample.selection_effects: Men who had stopped using MDMA and volunteered for a study a year or more later; people who went on to heavier use or developed problems are less likely to be in such a sample, and the groups were recruited separately rather than followed.

exposure.measurement: Semi-structured drug-history interview; urine screen on the scan day for MDMA, cocaine, amphetamine, opiates and benzodiazepines; hair samples covering a mean of 2.7 months (SD 0.9) tested for MDMA, cocaine and amphetamine, with two MDMA-positive people excluded (pp. 355-356).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Former MDMA group: mean 243.75 lifetime occasions (SD 244.4, range 60-864), 2.75 tablets in a typical session (1.9, range 1-8), 4.75 use days a month, 4.33 years of regular use, first use at 18.1 years (Table 1, p. 356).
exposure.polysubstance: Both drug-using groups continued to use other drugs and were matched on them: cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and LSD use did not differ between the MDMA and polydrug groups, with or without correction for multiple comparisons (Table 1, p. 356; Results, p. 357).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 3 days from recreational drugs, with urine and hair screening; mean time since last MDMA 2.74 years (SD 1.46; range given in days as 390-1825) (Table 1, p. 356).

comparison.controls: Two comparison groups: 9 men using a range of recreational drugs but never MDMA, and 19 men reporting no illicit drug use, of whom a random half gave urine and hair samples (pp. 355-356).
comparison.matching: The two drug-using groups were matched on reported drug and alcohol use; age differed across the three groups and was used as a covariate.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; the paper notes that a retrospective design cannot control for pre-existing differences (p. 357).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The polydrug group used cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and LSD at rates similar to the MDMA group; the drug-naive group reported none.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET on a high-sensitivity scanner, 90-min dynamic scan, arterial plasma input with metabolite correction, total distribution volume by graphical analysis, binding potential as the ratio to cerebellum; regions defined on co-registered MRI with a probabilistic atlas: amygdala, caudate, anterior and posterior cingulate, dorsal raphe, frontal cortex, hippocampus, insula, putamen, thalamus (pp. 356-357).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the transporter; the authors restrict cortical analysis to frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio in neocortex. No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Integrity of serotonin neurons is operationalized as regional binding potential; 'no long-term damage' as the absence of a significant group difference.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed for the primary analysis, which is a single repeated-measures model across regions; no regional post-hoc tests are reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures analysis of variance with age as covariate: main effect of brain region F=7.84 (df 9,324, p=0.002), no main effect of group (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, df 18,324, p=0.81); no effect of age (F=0.18, p=0.66). Cerebellar distribution volume did not differ (F=0.76, p=0.47), nor did injected dose or specific activity. No significant correlations between any variable of MDMA use and binding. The paper reports no regional means, differences or confidence intervals: the only regional data are the bar chart of Figure 1. A power statement says the study could have detected a 15-20% difference in binding potential in most regions at 80% power with p<0.05.
analysis.selective_reporting: Group results are reported only as a figure; the text gives no regional estimates, so a reader cannot see how close to or far from equality the groups were.
analysis.power: Stated as sufficient to detect a 15-20% difference in most regions at 80% power (p. 357); no observed effect sizes or intervals are given to check this, and the claim rests on unpublished variance estimates.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 men who had not used MDMA for at least a year, transporter binding did not differ significantly from that of 9 men who used other drugs or 19 men who used none, in 10 regions of which only one was neocortical.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the findings suggest MDMA use 'may not result in long-term damage to serotonin neurons when used recreationally in humans' (abstract, p. 355). The Discussion offers the alternative that binding recovered during abstinence and favours it, citing other studies. Neither can be distinguished here: there is no earlier measurement in these men, no group currently using MDMA and no equivalence analysis, and the one cortical region measured is not among those where other studies find the largest differences.

timeline.event: Lower binding in people abstinent on average 5 months, with a positive relation to months abstinent
Lower cortical and hippocampal binding at a median of 38 days of abstinence, with no relation to time since last use
Lower binding with a positive relation to days since last use in subcortical regions but not neocortex
Independent study noting that this study had no group of people currently using MDMA, so recovery cannot be inferred from it
Review counts this study among the evidence that binding recovers after abstinence

replication.where_it_stands: This is the only [11C]DASB study of people who had stopped, and the only one of six not to find lower cortical binding; whether that is recovery or a difference between samples is unresolved, since no study has scanned the same people during use and after long abstinence.

funding.funder: Medical Research Council; one author supported by an MRC studentship (Funding, p. 359).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declared: one author has received occasional consultancy from GlaxoSmithKline, Merck, Pfizer and GE Healthcare; one is an MRC clinical scientist; one is a GlaxoSmithKline employee and shareholder; one has served on speakers' panels for BMS, AstraZeneca and Janssen (p. 355).
funding.affiliations_note: MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, Hammersmith Hospital, with Oxford and University College London; the regions of interest were taken from the Baltimore group's earlier study.

what_would_settle_it: Scanning the same people while they are using MDMA and again after a year or more without it, with the occipital and temporal cortex included, and reporting regional estimates with intervals so that a null result can be read as equivalence rather than as absence of significance.

domains.note: Age differed between groups and was covaried; the polydrug comparison group addresses other drug use better than most studies in this field, but the groups are small and other confounders are not adjusted.

Lifetime occasions are self-reported; hair testing covered about 2.7 months and excluded two people with MDMA-positive hair, which supports the claim of abstinence but says nothing about historical doses.
Men only, recruited by advertisement a year or more after stopping; people with ongoing problems are unlikely to be represented, and the group that stopped may differ from those who continued.
Complete scans in all analysed participants.
Fully quantitative PET with arterial input, but only frontal cortex among neocortical regions, and the regions most affected in other studies (occipital, temporal) were not analysed.
No regional estimates or intervals are printed; the result is reported as a figure and a non-significant omnibus test, which makes the stated power claim uncheckable.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A null result from a small cross-sectional study whose regional values are not reported. It can be cited for the absence of a detectable group difference in men abstinent for at least a year, in the regions measured, and not for equivalence, for recovery, or for the neocortical regions it did not analyse.

key_findings.finding: No group effect on transporter binding (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, df 18,324, p=0.81); the only significant term was brain region (F=7.84, df 9,324, p=0.002).
Cerebellar distribution volume, injected dose and specific activity did not differ between groups (p=0.47, 0.13, 0.93), so the null result is not explained by tracer delivery.
No variable of MDMA use (lifetime occasions, typical session dose, duration, time since last use) correlated with binding.

The 12 men who had stopped had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions (SD 244, range 60-864), about 2.75 tablets per session, for a mean of 4.33 years, and had last used it a mean of 2.74 years earlier (SD 1.46).
Cortical analysis was restricted to the frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio of [11C]DASB in neocortex.
key_findings.locator: Method, 'Magnetic resonance scans and definition of volumes of interest', last paragraph
key_findings.note: Occipital and temporal cortex, where other [11C]DASB studies report the largest reductions, were not measured.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the study could have detected a 15-20% difference in binding potential in most regions at 80% power.
key_findings.note: No regional estimates, standard deviations or intervals are printed, so this cannot be checked; the only regional data are Figure 1, a bar chart with within-group standard deviations.

key_findings.finding: The groups did not differ in depression, anxiety, neuroticism or premorbid IQ (all p>0.2), and the two drug-using groups did not differ in cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine, LSD or alcohol use.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-way analyses of variance (age, cerebellar distribution volume, injected dose, specific activity) are reported with 2 and 39 degrees of freedom, which implies 42 participants, while the sample described is 40 (12 + 9 + 19) and the repeated-measures analyses use 2 and 36.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either two further people (perhaps the two excluded after MDMA-positive hair) were included in these tests, or the degrees of freedom are wrong; the group comparison of age, which justified using age as a covariate, is affected.

reporting_issues.issue: No regional means, group differences or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper; Figure 1 is the only source of regional values.
reporting_issues.consequence: A null finding cannot be read as equivalence without estimates and intervals; the paper's own power claim cannot be checked, and later sources can only record 'no difference'.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives time since last MDMA use as a mean in years with the range in days (390-1825, by footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the range corresponds to about 1.1 to 5 years, consistent with the inclusion criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that MDMA 'may not result in long-term damage' is drawn from a null result in 12 men, while the Discussion prefers the opposite explanation, that binding had recovered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract and the Discussion point in different directions; the study cannot distinguish them, since no one was scanned while using.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 355-359 plus the data supplement page (all pages; Figure 1 inspected on the rendered page 358 and no values read from it)
